---
title: "Methods"
description: "How each item of the OPDI data is computed from aircraft position reports, how it was checked, how accurate it is, and what its limits are."
---

The Open Performance Data Initiative (OPDI) turns aircraft position reports
into open data about flights. The reports come from the
[OpenSky Network](https://opensky-network.org/), a network of ground receivers
run by volunteers and research institutions. OPDI publishes, for each day, a
list of the flights and a list of events along those flights, with
measurements attached to the events.

This section explains, for each item of the data, how it is computed, what it
was compared with, how accurate it is and when it should not be used. It
describes release v2.0.0 and the default settings of the code that produced
it. The code is open: [euctrl-pru/opdi on GitHub](https://github.com/euctrl-pru/opdi).

## From position reports to flights

Aircraft send their position about once per second in **ADS-B** messages
(Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast). Each message identifies the
aircraft by its **ICAO 24-bit address**, a six-character code set in its
transponder, and usually by its **call sign**, the radio name of the flight
(for example `DLH123`). The OpenSky Network stores what it receives as
**state vectors**: one row per aircraft and second, with position, altitude,
speed, heading and vertical rate.

OPDI groups the state vectors of one aircraft into **tracks**. A track is the
run of state vectors that OPDI treats as one flight. Everything else is
computed per track. [Processing steps](pipeline.qmd) shows the whole chain.

## The data model

OPDI describes a flight with three kinds of information.

**Flight.** One row of the flight list per track. It gives the flight's
identifier (`flight_id`), the aircraft address and call sign, the date of
flight, the departure and destination airports, data about the aircraft from
the OpenSky aircraft database, and the main milestones of the flight, such as
the take-off and landing times and runways. A milestone column is empty when
the event behind it was not detected.

**Event.** A moment in a flight, such as the take-off, the top of climb or the
crossing of a flight level. Every event has:

- the flight it belongs to (`flight_id`);
- a position: longitude and latitude in degrees (WGS 84), and an altitude in
  feet;
- a time (`event_time`, in UTC);
- a **type**, for example `top-of-climb` or `xing-fir`;
- a **source**, the origin of the position data (`OSN` for the OpenSky
  Network);
- a **version**, which names the method that produced that event type. A
  method that changes gets a new version, so released data stay reproducible;
- **info**: extra details as JSON text, for example the runway of a take-off
  or the two regions of a FIR crossing.

Some things are not instants but periods, for example a level flight segment
or a holding pattern. They are published as a **pair of events**, one at the
start and one at the end (`level-start` and `level-end`, `holding-start` and
`holding-end`).

**Measurement.** A number attached to an event, published as a column of the
event's row. Two are given for nearly every event: the distance flown since
the start of the track (`distance_flown_nm`, in nautical miles) and the time
passed since then (`time_passed_s`, in seconds). Some event families add
their own, for example the time spent in a holding pattern. Because the
measurements are cumulative, subtracting the values of two events of one
flight gives the distance and time between them.

Units follow aviation use: altitudes in feet (ft), distances in nautical miles
(NM, 1 NM = 1,852 m), speeds in knots (kt, nautical miles per hour), vertical
rates in feet per minute and times in UTC.

## How to read a methods page

Every page about one item has the same nine sections, in the same order, so
that items can be compared.

| Section | What it says |
|---|---|
| What it is | The item in plain words, and where it appears in the data. |
| How it is computed | The method with the default settings of release v2.0.0, step by step, with every threshold and its unit. |
| Reference data | What the item was compared with, and for which days and places. |
| Validation method | How the comparison was made and which measures were used. |
| Results | The numbers the comparison gave. |
| Error distribution | A chart of how the errors are spread, where the study data allow one. |
| Headline accuracy | The single number to remember, with the number of cases behind it. |
| Limitations | When the item is missing, when it is wrong, and what not to conclude from it. |
| Full study | Links to the study reports with all details. |

An item that has not been validated keeps all nine sections and says "Not
validated" under them, with what would be needed to validate it.

Every number under Results and Headline accuracy comes from a file of results
committed with a study under `papers/`, and every chart is drawn from such
files. The table of all those numbers, with the file and column each comes
from, is [`assets/validation/validation_measures.csv`](../../assets/validation/validation_measures.csv).

## Measures used on these pages

- **Reference data** (or ground truth): an independent record of the same
  flights, used to check OPDI's answers. Most often this is EUROCONTROL
  Network Manager data, which cover flights in the European area.
- **Coverage**: of the reference cases, the share for which OPDI gives an
  answer.
- **Accuracy**: of the answers OPDI gives, the share that are right.
- **Precision**: of what OPDI reports, the share that the reference confirms.
- **Recall**: of what the reference holds, the share that OPDI finds.
- **F1 score**: one number that balances precision and recall (their harmonic
  mean); 1 is perfect.
- **Median** and **percentile**: half of the values are below the median;
  90% of the values are below the 90th percentile.
- **n**: the number of cases a result is computed over.
